intro:
Steakhouse phone reservations should be quick, clear, and easy for staff to manage. The same phone line can also handle takeout, as long as the call flow asks for the right details and sends the order to the kitchen cleanly.

For many steakhouses, the phone gets busy at the same time guests are trying to book a table and place a dinner order. ROAL can answer those calls, take pickup and delivery orders from the live menu, and pass reservation requests to staff with a summary. It works best when you keep the script short and the rules simple.

sections.h2: What details should a steakhouse ask on every phone call?
sections.body:
A steakhouse call should start with the reason for the call, then collect only the details that matter. For reservations, that usually means name, date, time, party size, and a callback number. For takeout, it means name, phone, items, modifiers, pickup time, and any notes that affect the kitchen.

Use a short script so callers do not drift into a long story. Example line: "Thanks for calling. Is this a reservation or a takeout order?" That one sentence saves time and helps you route the call correctly.

A simple call checklist:
- Reservation: name, date, time, party size, phone
- Takeout: name, phone, items, sizes, modifiers, pickup time
- Special notes: allergies, sauces on the side, no onions, extra utensils
- Final step: repeat the details back before ending the call

If you use ROAL, it can collect these details and send a clean ticket to the kitchen screen for orders. For reservation requests, it can gather the basics and hand the call to staff when needed.

sections.h2: How do you separate dinner reservations from takeout orders?
sections.body:
Steakhouses do best when reservations and takeout follow different paths. A reservation is a table problem. A takeout order is a kitchen problem. Mixing the two makes the front desk slower and creates errors.

A practical split looks like this:

| Call type | What to ask first | What happens next |
|---|---|---|
| Reservation | Name, time, party size | Confirm details and pass to staff if needed |
| Takeout | Name, phone, order items | Quote ready time and send to kitchen |
| Question only | Hours, address, parking, menu | Answer quickly and end the call |

Example script line: "For a table, I’ll get your name and time. For takeout, I’ll take the order and give you a pickup time." That makes the call feel organized without sounding stiff.

If your restaurant takes both dine-in and takeout, keep the phone host trained on both flows. ROAL can answer questions about hours, address, parking, and the menu, then take the order or reservation request from there. If the call gets tricky, it can send a summary to staff instead of guessing.

sections.h2: What should a steakhouse say about menu items, modifiers, and sold-out items?
sections.body:
Steakhouse orders often have more details than people expect. A guest may want a different temperature, sauce on the side, no butter, or a side swap. The phone script should make room for those notes without turning into a long interrogation.

A useful rule: ask for the item first, then the modifier, then the note. Example: "I have your ribeye. What size would you like? Any sides or changes?" That order keeps the call moving.

Use a simple modifier checklist:
- Size or cut
- Temperature, if your restaurant wants it taken by phone
- Side dish choice
- Sauce or topping changes
- Allergy-sensitive notes

If an item is sold out, do not offer it. ROAL follows that rule from the live menu, so the caller only hears items that are actually available. That matters on busy dinner nights when the kitchen runs low on popular cuts.

For a clean handoff, repeat the order in plain language: "That’s one 12-ounce ribeye, medium rare, mashed potatoes, and no mushrooms." A clear repeat-back is one of the easiest ways to avoid mistakes.

sections.h2: How should you set up call forwarding for a steakhouse?
sections.body:
Once the phone host is ready, the owner claims it and forwards the restaurant’s existing number to it. That can be all calls, or only when busy or unanswered. The restaurant keeps its own number, and forwarding can be turned off any time.

The exact steps depend on the carrier or phone system, so always confirm with your provider and test it with a live call. Common examples include these:

- Many landlines and some carriers: dial *72 plus the forwarding number to forward all calls, and *73 to turn it off
- Verizon Wireless: *72 / *73 for all calls, and *71 for busy or no-answer forwarding
- AT&T and T-Mobile GSM lines: **21*number# to forward all calls, ##21# to turn it off, **61*number# for unanswered calls, and **67*number# for busy calls
- Business VoIP systems: often set forwarding in the web portal

For reference, use [call forwarding codes by carrier](/tools/call-forwarding-codes). Then make a test call from a cell phone and from a landline, if you have one.

If you want the phone host to answer only after a few rings during dinner rush, that is often the easiest place to start. It keeps the front of house in control while still catching the calls that would otherwise go unanswered.

sections.h2: What should the front desk and kitchen see after the call ends?
sections.body:
A steakhouse phone call should end with a clean record, not a scribbled note. The front desk needs to know what was ordered or requested. The kitchen needs to see the ticket fast and in order.

ROAL includes a kitchen screen with live tickets marked new, preparing, and ready. It also keeps call history with transcripts and recordings, which helps you check what the caller said if a note needs review.

Here is a simple post-call checklist:
- Confirm the caller’s name and phone number
- Confirm the full order or reservation request
- Check for allergy-sensitive notes or special requests
- Make sure the ready time was quoted clearly
- Watch the ticket move to the kitchen screen

Example of a useful closing line: "You’re all set for 6:30 pickup. We’ll have your order ready then." That kind of line is short, calm, and easy for the guest to remember.

Questions the host could not answer go to an inbox. The owner answers once, and the host knows it from then on. That matters for steakhouse-specific questions about parking, private dining, holiday hours, or which cuts are available that night. takeaways: Steakhouse phone reservations work best when the call first separates reservations from takeout.
Ask for the few details the kitchen or host stand actually needs, then repeat them back.
A live menu helps avoid offering sold-out items by phone.

faq.q: How do I answer steakhouse phone reservations without slowing down takeout orders?
